cards.text: Annual incidence of aneurysmal SAH: {{c1::about 9.7–14.5 / 100,000}}; particularly high in {{c2::Finland (22.5 / 100,000)}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- Hypertension
- Smoking
- Excessive alcohol
- Sympathomimetic drugs (e.g., cocaine)

- Aneurysm in a first-degree relative / family history of SAH
- Known unruptured aneurysms
- Connective tissue disorders: **Ehlers–Danlos type IV**, **Marfan syndrome**, **polycystic kidney disease**

cards.text: Outcome after aneurysmal SAH (rule of thirds): about one-third {{c1::die}}, one-third {{c2::have moderate/severe permanent disability}}, one-third {{c3::return to baseline}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- Rebleeding
- Hydrocephalus (~15–20%)
- Cardiac complications (up to 50%)
- Vasospasm
- Hyponatremia
- Seizures

cards.titel: ISUIA: 5-year rupture risk of unruptured aneurysms (%)
cards.notiz: CNBR Table 6.1. Key point: posterior circulation and size ≥ 7 mm carry a much higher risk.

zeilen: Asymptomatic or minimal headache, slight nuchal rigidity
Moderate-to-severe headache, nuchal rigidity, ± cranial nerve palsy only
Drowsiness, confusion, or mild focal deficit
Stupor, moderate-to-severe hemiparesis, possibly early decerebrate rigidity
Deep coma, decerebrate rigidity, moribund appearance
cards.notiz: CNBR Table 6.2. Clinical vasospasm: grade I–III 20–30%, IV 50%, V 75%. Good outcome: I–III ~70%, IV ~15%, V ~0%.

cards.vorderseite: Fusiform aneurysm: definition and key feature
cards.rueckseite: Dilatation of the **entire circumference** of the vessel wall (vs. a localized bleb in saccular aneurysms), spindle-shaped. Presents like saccular aneurysms (SAH). Typically **not** amenable to conventional coiling or clipping.

Pseudoaneurysm: arterial rupture with hematoma contained by surrounding tissue. More often after **penetrating** than blunt head injury. Can lead to **carotid-cavernous fistula**. Often **delayed hemorrhage**. Treated surgically or endovascularly.

cards.text: Mycotic (infectious) aneurysms occur in {{c1::5–15%}} of patients with bacterial endocarditis, are usually {{c2::distal}}, and are mostly {{c3::fusiform and friable}}.

cards.rueckseite: Antibiotics; usually resolve within **6 weeks**. If still enlarging or not resolved on follow-up angiogram → associated with hemorrhage → **surgical treatment**.

Coiling vs. clipping for ruptured aneurysms: at **1 year**, large mortality/morbidity difference favoring **coiling**. At **5 years**, no mortality difference, but **more rebleeding and aneurysm recurrence** in the coiling group.
At 1 year, fewer poor outcomes with **coiling**; at 3 years, no difference. **Clipping** was better for recurrence, rebleeding and complete obliteration.

cards.vorderseite: AHA guidelines: when to favor coiling vs. clipping?
cards.rueckseite:
**Favor endovascular:** amenable to both, elderly patients, high-grade SAH (H&H IV–V), basilar apex.
**Favor surgery:** large associated ICH, MCA aneurysms, younger patients.

cards.text: Unruptured aneurysm, treatment risk: mortality {{c1::1–2%}}; morbidity about {{c2::4% for coiling}} and {{c3::8% for surgery}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- Most anterior circulation aneurysms: **pterional** (frontotemporal)
- AComA: may use anterior interhemispheric; distal ACA aneurysms: **must** use interhemispheric
- Basilar apex: pterional, subtemporal, or combined
Complex vascular lesion with **abnormal arteriovenous connections without an intervening capillary bed** and without neural tissue in the nidus.

cards.text: AVM presentation: {{c1::hemorrhage (50%)}}, {{c2::seizures (25%)}}, also headache, focal deficit (steal, venous hypertension), or incidental.
AVM hemorrhage risk: {{c1::2–4% per year}}; {{c2::6–18%}} in the first year after a hemorrhage (untreated). Mortality of a hemorrhage: {{c3::10–30%}}.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Grade I–II:** microsurgery (92–100% favorable outcomes)
- **Grade III:** radiosurgery, with adjunctive embolization
- **Embolization:** rarely curative alone (0–25%); presurgical, palliative, or curative for small deep lesions (Onyx/NBCA, 15–50%)
Pathological shunt between **meningeal or extracranial arteries** and a **dural venous sinus, dural veins, or cortical veins**.

zeilen: Dural sinus/vein drainage, no cortical venous reflux
Dural sinus drainage AND cortical venous reflux
cards.notiz: CNBR Table 6.7. Hemorrhage: type II 18% (6%/yr), type III 34% (10%/yr, 21%/yr with venous ectasia). Type I generally benign (conversion ~2%).

zeilen: Cortical reflux only, with venous ectasia

cards.vorderseite: DAVF: treatment goal and preferred treatment
cards.rueckseite: Goal: **eliminate cortical venous reflux**. Primarily endovascular, **transvenous coiling** generally preferred (transarterial embolization rarely cures). Alternatives: surgical disconnection, radiosurgery (~⅔ cure, third choice).

**Disease:** idiopathic stenosis/occlusion of the **supraclinoid ICA** with hypertrophy and proliferation of lenticulostriate collaterals.
**Syndrome:** same collaterals but with an **underlying cause** (e.g., atherosclerosis, radiation, sickle cell disease).

- **Asian children:** ischemia
- **Asian adults:** hemorrhage
- **North American:** adults 30–50 y, F > M, mostly ischemia, more often unilateral

- Direct: **STA–MCA bypass**
- Indirect: encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis (EDAS), encephaloduroarteriomyosynangiosis (EDAMS)
- Omental transposition, multiple burr holes

Multilobulated vascular malformation of **endothelium-lined caverns without mature vessel walls**. Low-flow, **angiographically occult**. May be associated with a **developmental venous anomaly (DVA)**.

cards.text: Cavernous malformation: prevalence {{c1::0.5%}}; familial forms are {{c2::autosomal dominant (CCM1–3)}}, particularly prevalent in the {{c3::Hispanic population}}.
Cavernous malformation: symptomatic hemorrhage risk {{c1::0.5–2% per year}}; higher after prior hemorrhage (~{{c2::5%/yr}}) and in deep lesions (~{{c3::10%/yr}}).

cards.rueckseite: Does **not** change the radiographic appearance and has **not been shown** to alter natural history (may modestly reduce seizure risk). Treatment for recurrent hemorrhage/seizures: **surgical excision** (~90% good/excellent outcome).

cards.vorderseite: ICH: most common cause overall and in the elderly
cards.rueckseite: Overall: **hypertension**. In the elderly: **cerebral amyloid angiopathy**.

- **STICH I/II:** surgery for supratentorial ICH, only very mild long-term mortality benefit
- **MISTIE:** minimally invasive aspiration + tPA, ~50% clot reduction, more patients with mRS 0–3
- **CLEAR:** tPA via EVD for IVH, mortality 18% vs. 23%

Edema → **brainstem compression** and **obstructive hydrocephalus** (mainly 12–96 h after ictus, mortality up to 80%). With early symptoms: **emergent suboccipital craniectomy**/removal of infarcted tissue; EVD only as a temporizing measure.

Malignant edema in up to 10% (mortality up to 80%). Early hemicraniectomy reduces mortality by ~30–40%, but morbidity remains severe. Better outcomes in younger patients and nondominant hemisphere. Trials: **HAMLET, DESTINY, DECIMAL**.

cards.titel: Carotid stenosis: CEA vs. best medical therapy

cards.vorderseite: Carotid stenosis: indications and timing of CEA
cards.rueckseite:
- **Symptomatic 70–99%:** CEA indicated
- **Symptomatic 50–69%** or **asymptomatic 60–99%:** consider (careful selection, low perioperative risk)
- Timing: preferably **within 2 weeks** (risk is front-loaded, 20% in the first month)
- Stenting (CREST): stroke/death rate about double that of CEA
Headache/neck pain, **Horner syndrome**, TIA/stroke. Cerebral or retinal ischemia in 50–95%.

cards.vorderseite: Modified Denver criteria (screening for blunt cerebrovascular injury)
cards.rueckseite:
- Lateralizing deficit not explained by CT
- Infarct on CT
- Cervical hematoma, epistaxis
- Horner syndrome
- GCS < 8 with negative CT
- Cervical spine fracture, basilar skull fracture, severe facial fracture
- Cervical bruit/thrill
- Seatbelt sign above the clavicle

cards.text: Intracranial vertebrobasilar dissection presenting with SAH: rebleed rate {{c1::30–70%}}, with {{c2::70% in the first 24 h}}.

cards.rueckseite:
**Direct** (high-flow, usually traumatic or ruptured cavernous ICA aneurysm): pain, chemosis, **pulsatile proptosis**, bruit, visual loss, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia.
**Indirect** (low-flow, dural branches of ICA/ECA): insidious onset, **conjunctival injection** most prominent.

cards.text: About {{c1::75%}} of carotid-cavernous fistulas are traumatic; they occur in up to {{c2::4%}} of basilar skull fractures.

cards.rueckseite: Low-flow: may observe for spontaneous thrombosis if visual acuity stable and **intraocular pressure < 25 mm Hg** (± manual compression of the cervical ICA). Otherwise endovascular: transarterial (balloon, trapping) or **transvenous** via inferior petrosal sinus or superior ophthalmic vein. Open surgery rarely.
